units.title: Primary and permanent teeth
units.lesson: The typical primary dentition contains 20 teeth. A complete permanent dentition can contain 32 when third molars are included. These are reference counts, not a requirement that every individual has exactly that number. Eruption, missing teeth and other variation matter. Use the terms primary, mixed and permanent to describe developmental context.
units.question: What is the typical primary dentition count?
rationales: 32 refers to complete permanent dentition including third molars.
This is the primary reference count.
This is not the complete primary reference count.

units.title: Adapt communication to the child
units.lesson: AAPD describes behaviour guidance as an ongoing, individualized process. Effective communication and understanding the child’s needs matter. Medical history, temperament, pain, previous experiences and the proposed care influence planning. The same explanation will not fit every child. This academic introduction does not teach sedation, restraint or pharmacological behaviour management.
units.question: Which approach matches individualized behaviour guidance?
choices: Use the same script regardless of the child
Consider communication, pain and previous experiences
Assume silence proves understanding
units.explanation: Planning should reflect the child and relevant circumstances.
rationales: This ignores individual needs.
These are relevant documented factors.
Silence does not establish understanding.

units.title: Risk assessment is not a diagnosis
units.lesson: Caries-risk assessment considers biological and social context, protective factors and clinical findings. Risk concerns the likelihood of disease development or progression; it is not identical to counting existing cavities. A child with no currently visible cavity still has a risk profile. Assessment tools organize evidence rather than guarantee an individual outcome.
units.question: Which distinction is correct?
choices: Risk predicts possibility; current disease findings describe present status
Risk and cavity count always mean exactly the same thing
No visible cavity means no risk can exist
units.explanation: Risk and current disease status answer different questions.
rationales: This separates future likelihood and current findings.
They are not identical measures.
Absence of a finding does not eliminate future risk.

units.title: Explain mineral loss simply
units.lesson: Caries involves acid generated by plaque bacteria using fermentable dietary substrates. Repeated acid challenges can favour mineral loss. For an educational explanation, connect substrate, biofilm activity and tooth surface response. Do not reduce caries to a child being “careless” or assume a single habit explains every case.
units.question: Which chain describes a caries mechanism?
choices: Plaque acid challenge → mineral loss
Tooth name → enamel growth
Crown colour → guaranteed diagnosis
units.explanation: Bacterial acid production can favour demineralization.
rationales: This states the relevant mechanism.
A name is not a biological cause.
Colour alone is not a diagnosis.

units.question: A textbook gives 32 as the complete permanent reference count. Which qualification is correct?
choices: Every adult must have exactly 32 erupted teeth
The count excludes all permanent molars
The count includes third molars and is not universal for every individual
units.explanation: The standard complete count includes third molars; individual dentition can differ.
rationales: This turns a reference count into an absolute claim.
Molars are included.
This gives the reference count’s scope.
units.hint: Check which teeth the count includes.

units.question: A paper history describes a child’s pain and a difficult previous visit. How should a guidance plan use this information?
choices: Treat it as irrelevant to communication
Include it among factors informing individualized guidance
Infer a sedative dose from history alone
units.explanation: Pain and prior experience are relevant planning factors, not sufficient information for a drug instruction.
rationales: These factors can affect communication.
This uses the history within its proper role.
The information does not establish a dose.
units.hint: Use history without inventing a treatment.

units.title: Risk assessment is not a diagnosis · apply
units.lesson: Close the notes. Apply the concept to this new example, then compare your reasoning with the explanation.
units.question: A fictional child has no current recorded cavity but several relevant risk factors. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: Future disease is impossible
Risk assessment can still be relevant
A precise future cavity count is certain
units.explanation: Current findings and future disease likelihood are different questions.
rationales: No present finding does not eliminate future risk.
Risk can be assessed before visible disease.
Risk assessment does not guarantee an exact outcome.
units.hint: Avoid certainty from an empty count.

units.question: Which explanation best connects diet and caries without claiming one factor determines every outcome?
choices: Diet alone guarantees the same outcome in every child

units.explanation: Caries mechanisms and risk involve interacting factors.
rationales: This ignores individual and protective factors.
This preserves the multifactorial mechanism.
